The thing about this story, is that you find out something that feels like a big plot twist and really enhances your understanding, and then that just keeps happening. There are a lot of aha moments here, like a lot. 
How the mechanics work mean that this game isn't necessarily all that difficult which can be nice because then there isn't too much frustration. Might bug people who want to feel more skilled for figuring things out, because creativity is a very helpful thing here. You find videos by searching up words, and honestly sometimes my ideas would build up faster than I had time to search them, and then I would write them down as tags in a stored video. One thing to note there, whatever tags you have does actually affect it's ability to come up in the search, which matters because only 5 of the entries with that word can come up. That does seem a bit weird, because I am not really incentivized to tag things properly if it's going to get in the way of my search. Also leads to an exploit in finding more videos that gets pointed out in some guides.
Only thing is that the ending doesn't actually seem to require that you really understand what is happening. I thought I had a pretty good idea, but yet again, I was wrong. Since your understanding does keep changing, I did not really understand, looking back. But hey, I get it, probably wanted to have the database discovery achievements mean more, and making finding them all after the credits easier does mean there needs to be stuff remaining.

I think I may have slightly ruined this game for myself by accidently stumbling upon the ending video early. Then again, I suppose that's just the nature of the format - the rough must be taken with the smooth, etc. etc., and I am of the opinion that more games should be experimenting with nonlinear storytelling.

Recommended with the caveats that it is (1) extremely short and (2) a bit underbaked in terms of design. Play this if you are interested in the design of detective games that dare to thread in experimental waters.

In 'her story', you attempt to solve a case by spitting through hours of police interview footage of a woman under question. The game uses live FMV footage of an actress. You cannot watch the footage sequentially, instead, you have to search the interview for certain keywords to see how they are mentioned. This creates an entirely non-lineair way of experiencing the story. Reminiscent of 'Return of the Obra Dinn' or 'Case of the Golden Idol'.

I love the dedication to non-linearity: There are no gated clips or footage, the experience of the story is entirely guided by your curiosity, which makes it an almost frictionless puzzlebox to uncover. However, I now discover why these guardrails are generally in place, since one trope-savvy keyword search unveiled the major twist to me within 10 minutes of playing the game. Non-linearity has no respect for a dramatic structure. A similar thing happened with solving the crime, but here I just stumbled upon the most incriminating message, which undid al the sleuthing I had done in reconstructing the crime.

The game also doesn't have any true mechanic on solving the crime. Instead, a prompt will show up and politely ask you if you feel like you have gotten what you wanted from the experience, which is slanted more through the question if you have an emotional understanding of the case rather than a judicial one. I actually preferred how 'Obra Dinn' makes its questions purely judicial and leaves the sympathies and moralities entirely to the player. That both made a wry political statement as well as permitting the freedom of the player.

The game permits enough freedom, but so much that it doesn't feel like the game properly entices you to solve the case. It is missing goalposts and that has an effect on engagement, even if designing such goalposts for a detective game can be a real headache. 

That approach to case design based on your emotional connection is also very dependent on how actually emotionally engaging the case is. Overall, the actress does a fine job but the overall production feels a little cheap. There are some charming, offhand moments to find but they are too few and far between. The actual story is also very convoluted in a way that those detective stories can be, with the world inexplicably functioning like a rube goldberg machine which a lot of words are spilled on to justify its logic. 

In general, I think it should have leaned into the campy elements more or gone full procedural and grounded. 

That doesn't sound that positive now does it? Well, sometimes a strong experiment can do a lot! If you approach this like an impressive attempt of creating an immersive 'black story' (you know that card game), you will have a lot of fun with it to figure it out in a short, breezy evening.

Her Story encontra força na forma como transforma pesquisa em investigação. A mecânica de buscar palavras-chave nos vídeos do interrogatório é muito criativa e faz o jogador participar ativamente da descoberta, porque não basta só assistir: é preciso prestar atenção aos detalhes para refinar as buscas e abrir novos caminhos. A história vai se montando aos poucos na cabeça, como um quebra-cabeça, e essa sensação de juntar as peças por conta própria é o que torna a experiência tão envolvente.

A narrativa fragmentada também é parte essencial disso. Se a história fosse contada de forma linear, dificilmente teria o mesmo impacto. Do jeito que foi construída, cada jogador acaba chegando às revelações por um caminho diferente, o que dá uma identidade muito própria para a investigação. Além disso, a própria história é interessante o suficiente para sustentar esse formato e fazer com que cada nova descoberta pareça relevante.

A atuação ajuda muito a vender essa proposta. Os vídeos praticamente carregam o jogo inteiro, e a performance funciona bem o bastante para passar a sensação de que estamos realmente assistindo a um interrogatório. O jogo também é muito bem pensado na forma como recorta essas gravações e organiza a mecânica de busca, sempre com o cuidado de manter o jogador engajado e curioso para descobrir qual é o próximo passo.

O ponto fraco é que boa parte do interesse está concentrada no mistério principal. Depois que ele é resolvido, o incentivo para continuar cai bastante, e o que sobra é mais curiosidade por detalhes do que vontade real de seguir investigando. Ainda assim, o jogo deixa uma impressão forte justamente por fazer algo muito simples de um jeito bastante criativo.

[b]Nota: 8/10[/b]

[spoiler]Her Story is a modern day fairy tale turned true crime podcaster's wet dream. Twin sisters, separated at birth, live a shared life of secrets and connection, until it all falls apart. The narrative I've seen described as complex, but it felt largely simple, if a bit silly, when it came down to it. A stolen baby, two girls sharing one life, jealousy and separation, reunion, an affair, a pregnancy, a murder. 

Is it true? Maybe. Probably not exactly as it was said, but there are elements that are easy enough to verify- a tattoo, an alibi- that make me dubious of theories of DiD or the second self being a fabrication to escape culpability. 

I think this is, in fact, trying to stick to the fairy tale conceit it references enough to be almost hammering you over the head with it. If I were to describe the plot in flowery language, it would sound very similar to an old and dark fable, one teaching the value of sharing and following rules by a representation of the tragedy that comes from breaking them. To that end, it’s true- and it’s magical. To try and pin this down to reality, despite the grounded nature of the crime drama presentation and mothballed tech, to attempt to turn this into purely a mystery to be solved, is to lose what this game is actually attempting to do. 

A silver mirror. A girl in the attic. A stolen baby. Rapunzel and Arabian Nights and the Princess and the Pauper. It’s a story about stories, as trite as that may sound. What impressed me the most about that fact is that it is a story that challenges the person to analyze by necessity, to engage with it in a way you would not with a film. This is done, of course, through its core investigation mechanic and structure of being broken up into little clips, but also through the genre it masquerades as. In crime stories, something happened. In crime investigation games, your job is to figure out what that thing is. In many of those games, there is a truth you can reach or fall short of. So you pay attention. You scrutinize inconsistencies. You notice patterns. You perform narrative analysis as you play the game, you play it to experience the story, you can’t start after, it’s a constructive process within the experience itself. The search for truth runs you directly into exploring the magic. 

That’s a clever trick! I doubt it bats a thousand. That same pursuit can create a tunnel vision, a frustration with inconsistency, a feeling of false promise that was left unfulfilled, a refusal to bend with the genre and having the experience break as a result. 

I played this after Immortality, and I don't know if that helped or hurt it. Immortality is larger, a more ambitious project with a more supernatural narrative, a very explicit one at that. I think one benefit of playing Immortality first was that the magical realism of Her Story was an expected aspect to me on a subconscious level, so I didn’t fight it, even if that magic is far more metaphorical here than in Immortality. Immortality’s investigation system had its advantages and disadvantages as well- while momentum could be built through brute force if nothing else was working there in a way it’s harder to here, the directed control, the action and result, the sense of AGENCY in the process is far superior in Her Story. Still, I stalled out without completing the footage gallery of either game.

For Her Story, I stopped after finding around 80% of clips, but felt I had the full story, or close enough to it that the rest was just details, by 50%. There was more to learn after that point, sure, but I never had any moments of revelation past that time, which disappointed me. Just shy of a hundred minutes and I’d cracked it, with half the road left to run. Details of the affair added a bit more context, but I quickly felt I had run out of mysteries I wanted answers to (outside of the deaths of the parents), or details I felt compelled to fill in. It’s a fairy tale after all, every telling is a bit different, taking different parts to compile a similar whole. 

There is, content wise, a disappointingly misogynistic undertone for me. In Immortality, the commodification of women’s sexuality felt like it was doing something, or at least trying to, most of the time, through its narrative about the predatory nature of the film industry. Here, the feeling is just… strange. Eve didn’t need to “take Hannah’s virginity” with a hairbrush, Hannah could’ve done that herself. Hannah and Simon getting married because she got pregnant at 17 is one thing, having Eve go ♥♥♥♥ random adult men in alleys to try and get pregnant to match until she got an STI is another. It feels gross, and like its intention is to be as such. This in all, has an atonal effect on the rest of the story- revolting exceptions to the modern fairy tale structure, things that would be out of place even in the Grimm inspirations they draw from, as they do not feel they serve a purpose. 

Her Story is a pretty tight, focused, and well executed experience. It’s one I do have respect for both the craft and cultural impact of. It did not knock my socks off, but I was overall impressed, and it got me to think about themes. That’s a challenge many games fail to meet. [/spoiler]
